# . Min Jin Lee Was Underestimated... - Jaya Bhattacharji Rose | Facebook
## Jaya Bhattacharji Rose's Post
“Smell that?” The novelist Min Jin Lee closed her eyes and drew in a breath. Garlic, ginger, turmeric, old floor polish, stale sweat, rat poison, glass cleaner, oregano. “It doesn’t smell like that on the Upper East Side,” she said with a laugh.
We were standing in the foyer of the apartment building on Van Kleeck Street, in Queens, where Lee lived with her parents and two sisters after they arrived from Korea in 1976. Everything looked the same: the dull metal mailboxes, the checkered linoleum in the hallway, the dusty glass wall facing the street. Only the names marking the buzzers had changed. In Lee’s childhood, they were mostly Irish, Greek and Eastern European. Now they were mostly Latino, Korean and Chinese.
The first thing that struck Lee about her new home was its ugliness. In Seoul, her mother kept their home impeccable. In Queens, their first rental was a one-bedroom furnished with grimy rugs, roaches and mice. Even at 7 years old, she understood that her family’s move to New York meant that they’d come down in the world.
In Seoul, they lived in a comfortable house in a middle-class neighborhood. Her father worked as a marketing executive. Her mother, who had studied music at Korea’s prestigious Yonsei University, taught children piano. But her father, who lost his home and most of his family as a teenager during the Korean War of the 1950s, feared that the violence of the Vietnam War might spread to South Korea and hurt his children. A relative in New York sponsored the family for visas, and they decamped for America, where her parents eventually found work in a wholesale jewelry shop in Midtown Manhattan. Every morning except Sunday they left the apartment at 6 to catch the subway, while the girls readied themselves for school alone.
For Lee, the move proved a social nightmare. In Korea, she’d been a peaceful introvert, the kind of child who often sat alone daydreaming. In America, she became a target. Tall, shy, not yet fluent in English, dressed in hand-me-downs, she was bullied ruthlessly for five years, starting in second grade.

## Jaya Bhattacharji Rose's Post
“I was like a mark,” Lee recalled. “It was just like, You want to pick the big, goofy, quiet one.” Terrified, she turned nearly mute in public.
At home, though she was loved, she also felt there was something wrong with her. Her two sisters immediately tested into top academic classes, while she was tracked into the lowest classes for two years. Her father nicknamed her Turtle.
She had one superpower. At the age of 3, Lee taught herself to read. And in Queens, she discovered America’s great, humble treasure: the public library system. For an immigrant girl with no money, nowhere to go and no friends besides her sisters, the existence of a place that would lend her as many books as she wanted — for free! — was paradise. She read endlessly, rolling volumes home in a collapsible shopping cart. “A book only gives,” she explained to me. As a girl reading, she felt “infinite.” She became especially well versed in the classics of American and European literature, because those were the books the librarians recommended.
Now 57, Lee is considered one of the most important novelists of her generation — and a torch bearer for the great 19th-century tradition of social realism. Like George Eliot, she has a gift for combining intimate character portraits with sweeping macroeconomic narratives. Like Charles Dickens, she seems determined to expose the indignities of poverty and the resilience needed to survive them.

## Jaya Bhattacharji Rose's Post
But even as she inherited her tools from these social realists, she uses them in modern ways to chronicle the lives of Koreans around the world. She set her first novel, “Free Food for Millionaires” (2007), among the Korean diaspora in New York City. The book’s central character, Casey Han, lives on Van Kleeck Street, until she escapes to Princeton and Manhattan. Lee’s second novel, “Pachinko” (2017), is a saga about four generations of Koreans. Set in colonial and post-colonial Japan, the novel is grounded in interviews that Lee conducted with elderly Koreans around Osaka and Tokyo. For her, “Pachinko” was a passion project; she never believed that it would find a big readership. After it was published, however, the novel became a global best seller and a critical sensation. In 2024, The New York Times Book Review ranked “Pachinko” No. 15 on its “100 Best Books of the 21st Century.”
“The fact that I can make that interesting to a general audience is really just a testament to what all those dead writers have taught me,” Lee told me. Her third novel, “American Hagwon,” debuted this month. Set in Korea, Australia and California during the years surrounding the Asian financial crisis of 1997, it contains more than a dozen characters from several interconnected families. The word “hagwon” means “private tutoring center” in Korean, and the novel examines how an unbridled obsession with gaining admission to name-brand universities may damage both parents and children. Among the book’s characters are parents who erase their savings paying for hagwons, teachers who coach SAT prep at hagwons and a young girl whose parents abandon her in California with the expectation that she will study hard, get accepted to U.C.L.A. and become a doctor — so that she can save her family in Korea from poverty.

## Jaya Bhattacharji Rose's Post
Lee (left) as a child arriving in the United States with her family for the first time in March 1976.Credit...From Min Jin Lee
For Lee, fiction has always been a way to wrestle with big social and historical dilemmas. Unlike many novelists, she begins her books with ideas and issues, not characters and scenes. Her chosen medium — the class-crossing realist narrative — has a long history as a weapon of social critique. Edith Wharton used it to savage the hypocrisies of old-money New York. Upton Sinclair used it to provoke reform in the slaughterhouses of Chicago. In “American Hagwon,” Lee herself is trying to shift the way we understand the purpose of higher education and to demonstrate how seemingly crazy behavior, like dropping off a 9-year-old in a foreign country, may be driven by a tremendous sense of fear and economic impotence.
When I asked Lee about the possibility of writing as a form of self-expression, she winced. “That’s not even interesting to me,” she said. “It sounds sort of corny, but if I didn’t think that these stories had value to my reader, I would never share it. Never.”
“History has failed us, but no matter.” The first line of “Pachinko” is a declaration of resilience and defiance, the pronouncement of someone who knows the score yet still forges ahead. The sentence is often interpreted as an indictment of the way historians tend to ignore the less-documented lives of the poor and the defeated. It may also be read as a wry summary of Lee’s own journey to “Pachinko.”

In college, she never planned on becoming a novelist. Her great intellectual romance, discovered at the Bronx High School of Science, was with history. For her, history was a way of trying to understand how the world worked, and how the circumstances of the present day were created by decisions made in the past. At Yale, she was mesmerized by the lectures given in the department’s survey courses, and she fantasized about getting a doctorate in the subject.

## Jaya Bhattacharji Rose's Post
Inspired by classes that she took in African American studies and women’s studies, Lee spearheaded a campaign to persuade Yale to offer courses in Korean language and history. She had the ingenious idea of asking students to petition their parents for the changes rather than plead with the administration directly. One of these parents, she said, ultimately raised $100,000 for a pilot program. More than 20 years later, Yale still teaches Korean language as a result of these efforts.
Despite this triumph, Lee’s affair with history ended badly. During her junior year, the university finally offered the class on Korean history that she’d longed for. But when the professor returned her midterm exam, she felt socked. Lee’s blue book, she told me, contained no guiding corrections or annotations. On its last page, there was only one handwritten line — “Ah, me, what’s to say?” — next to the letter F.
Most of the students crying near her in class that day were Asian. So Lee asked the professor, a white man who specialized in Japanese history, for a demographic breakdown of the grades. When he presented it at the following class, it was clear that most of the students he’d failed were, in fact, Asian. The reason, he said, was that they were STEM majors. Outraged by his assumptions, Lee published an article in a campus newspaper detailing the incident. It raised a furor at Yale. A white student labeled her a politically correct “terrorist.” After that, she told me, students and professors in the history department regarded her as a troublemaker.
“I think my heartbreak was proportionate with how much I really wanted the class, which sounds so dorky,” Lee told me. She wasn’t worried about her grades. What she wanted was to be treated with respect. She passed the class, but after the scandal she couldn’t stomach approaching any professor in the department for a recommendation to a doctoral program.

## Jaya Bhattacharji Rose's Post
Instead, Lee pivoted to a practical future: She went to law school at Georgetown. There she fell in love with a bank salesman, Christopher Duffy. For a year, she hid the relationship from her parents because Duffy is half-Japanese. “If you marry him, you are not my daughter,” her father said, when she told him that they were engaged. But Duffy was the kindest man that Lee had ever met, and ultimately he won over her father as well.
Lee married Duffy after her graduation and began working as a corporate lawyer in Manhattan, specializing in mergers and acquisitions. As a junior member of a firm, she read thousands of pre-existing contracts, combing them for liabilities that might hurt clients after they closed a deal. “I was really good at this,” she said, “because once you tell me to turn every page, I’m like, Yes, I’ll turn every page.” She wore suits, earned more than $80,000 a year and worked seven days a week. In theory, she was living the American dream. In practice, she was growing seriously ill.
Image
A black-and-white photograph from the 1980s showing a young Asian woman sitting alone inside a graffiti-covered NYC subway car leafing through a book.
Lee on the subway in 1985 heading from Bronx High School of Science to her home in Queens.Credit...John McGrail
In high school, after donating blood, Lee learned that she was an inactive chronic carrier for the liver disease hepatitis B. Though she never smoked or drank alcohol, the condition flared acutely during her sophomore year of college. A doctor at Yale New Haven Hospital told her that she would probably develop liver cancer by her early 30s. With luck, he said, she might get a transplant and be cured. After that consult, Lee feared that she might die young. Then, at 26, the long hours of corporate law were leaving her wrecked with exhaustion. She decided that she’d rather try writing fiction.

## Jaya Bhattacharji Rose's Post
At Yale, Lee had won two literary prizes: one for short fiction, the other for an essay. When she initially submitted the same essay to a history professor, he gave it a C and suggested that she needed remedial English tutoring. But the literary contests were hosted by the university’s English department, which scrubbed students’ names from their entries before judging. Her wins surprised her and came with such ease that they misled her into believing that writing a great novel would be less challenging than practicing law. She thought it might take her a year to finish a book and start earning roughly the same as she had reading contracts. Instead, completing the manuscript for “Free Food for Millionaires” took 11 years.
During that time, Lee’s writing earned her approximately nothing. She and Duffy, meanwhile, accumulated the joyous responsibility of caring for their first child and the unexpected necessity of supporting his parents through catastrophic debt. Her acute hepatitis recurred, making her wrists so weak that she had trouble lifting coffee cups. In a prologue to the 10th-anniversary edition of “Free Food for Millionaires,” she remembers her apprenticeship as an extended humiliation. “It is never a financially prudent idea to be a fiction writer,” she explains. “After six years, I had not yet written a published novel, and I was broke from the choices I had made.”
Because she was young and liver transplants were hard to obtain, a gastroenterologist suggested that she try an experimental drug: Interferon alfa. The treatment made her hair fall out and provoked unpredictable vomiting and diarrhea. But less than a year after starting it, she was miraculously cured.

## Jaya Bhattacharji Rose's Post
At the same time, she kept trying to compose the kind of juicy, realist book that enthralled her as a child. Lee often names “dead writers” as her teachers, including Leo Tolstoy, George Eliot, Edith Wharton, the Bröntes, Willa Cather, F. Scott Fitzgerald and James Baldwin. She read, reread and reverse-engineered their books. But in her prologue to “Free Food for Millionaires,” Lee recognizes that a host of contemporary authors taught her, as well. She took classes at the Asian American Writers’ Workshop and the 92nd Street Y in New York City, and participated in a private workshop with several aspiring writers, including the novelist Sharon Pomerantz, who remains a close friend. “You could look back on it with nostalgia,” Pomerantz said of this period in their lives, “but I think we were both filled with terror.”
From her legal experience, Lee carried over two unfashionable traits. The first was an attitude of advocacy. “This is the one part about being a lawyer I didn’t mind,” she told me. “I was arguing for somebody else.” All her novels are composed in defense of the overlooked, the tormented, the powerless. Though she published “Pachinko” a decade after “Free Food for Millionaires,” she worked on both books simultaneously. In one, Lee exposed the pressures and hypocrisies that Korean professionals faced in New York City. In the other, she laid bare an entire history of discrimination against Koreans in Japan. She felt as if she needed to write these stories for the sake of other Koreans, and this sense of responsibility kept her researching and revising even when the tasks she set for herself seemed absurdly hard.
“I would love to have that sort of freedom of saying, Oh, I don’t care what I stand for, but whether I like it or not, I do represent a group,” she said. “People still see you as the envelope that you’re in, whether you like it or not.”

## Jaya Bhattacharji Rose's Post
The setting is an influential Presbyterian megachurch in Seoul’s fashionable Gangnam neighborhood. Its main pastor, an affable, 50-something man, is preaching on the sin of idolatry. His sermon opens with Leviticus: the Israelites who disobeyed God by sacrificing their children to a pagan deity. “What do you love more than your child?” the pastor asks his rich congregants. “What do you love more than God?”
His questions resonate throughout “American Hagwon,” but in this chapter, Lee treats them lightly, directing our attention mostly away from the pulpit and toward the pews.
A pair of sisters, Helen and Sonya, sit near each other with their two husbands, their five children and a father-in-law. Lee establishes their back story in two tight paragraphs. As girls, they “lived at subsistence level.” Their parents were gamblers, and they survived on charity from the Catholic Church. After they graduated from a prestigious women’s college, the gorgeous Sonya went to work for a real estate baron, who married her to his nephew. At the church, Sonya sports an elegant cashmere suit with “a thick rope of rare Tahitian pearls.” Helen wears a fancy wool suit that’s getting a little tight; Sonya bought it for her years earlier. Another woman, Nari, appears near the end of the chapter with her daughter. When Nari stands next to the sisters, she realizes that her expensive red dress with “dramatic black sequin flowers” looks tacky in church. She introduces Helen to the idea of sending her children to a budget-breaking hagwon.
These scenes don’t feel especially significant the first time you read them. But within a few hundred pages, two of these characters will be broke and working at a fried-fish joint in California. Another pair will be entangled in an eye-popping affair. Two acquaintances will have turned into best friends. And the six children will have attended five different universities on three different continents. One of them will drop out.

## Jaya Bhattacharji Rose's Post
These are the techniques that Lee gleaned from the old social realists: intricately braided story lines, characters who cross social classes, an emphasis on plots that expose true morals. Many also deployed a nearly invisible third-person narrator. In “American Hagwon,” this device is so neutral as to be disconcerting. Flaubert eyed his characters — even those based on himself — with sly condescension. Dickens regarded his with sticky sentimentality. Lee’s vision is like bright, afternoon light; it casts no shadows. The rhythm of her sentences is conversational, and their diction is deliberately plain, barely adorned. It’s as if she wants to make reading her long, complicated novel as easy as possible, knowing that its most moving effects are felt not in the paragraphs but across the arc of chapters.
In college, Lee spent her most meaningful hours hanging out in the basement of Durfee Hall, where students of color held gatherings at the women’s center. The legacy of those sustaining female friendships appears in her work, where women are often rescued from hardship and despair by other women. In this sense, Lee’s books have more in common with Elena Ferrante’s Neapolitan novels than with anything by Eliot or Wharton.
“There’s a lot of different ways to circumvent patriarchy, because it’s such a heavy machinery,” Lee told me. “Whatever oppressive system you have, we get around it through other interpersonal relationships.”
Lee’s next novel is likely to push this theme even further. In our conversations, she referred to it as her “Marshall Plan book.” It would explore, she said, how the post-World War II rise of South Korea in the 1960s was underwritten by remittances sent home by Koreans living abroad, including culture-crossing wives. “When we think about all the glamour and beauty of South Korea today, we don’t think about all the bar girls who married G.I.s, who lived in Texas, and people called them hookers,” Lee said. “But if it weren’t for them, they wouldn’t have sponsored citizenship for their cousins and their brothers and sent money back for their education.”

## Jaya Bhattacharji Rose's Post
It was hard for Lee to think about these women because it was so upsetting how they were mistreated. They sacrificed so much and, in return, they were slurred by other Koreans. It was too outrageous. She’d already begun filling a set of floor-to-ceiling shelves in her office with volumes of research.
One afternoon, Lee and I stood on Queens Boulevard staring at the Gothic face of the First Presbyterian Church of Newtown in Elmhurst. “This is the church I grew up in,” Lee said. “I remember thinking it was so much bigger.”
The bell tower seemed to waver in the July heat. In front, a wrought-iron gate was padlocked but a side door was cracked open. We slipped in.
“Nothing has changed,” Lee said, as she took a seat. Rib-like ceiling trusses graced a soaring ceiling; the stained-glass windows shimmered. The nave held no more than 20 pews. It smelled of wood polish and old velvet.
You could call this sanctuary Lee’s most important school. Together with her family, she attended services and youth groups, ate coffee cake and doughnut holes. Back then, the congregation was mostly Anglo American, but at Sunday school, unlike elementary school, people were nice to her.
Churches have always played a central function in Lee’s fiction. Her halls of worship allow characters to swap information, forge friendships, rustle up business, preserve their traditions and repair the damage done to their dignity by the turbulence of emigration. But sitting next her in the silence of First Presbyterian — seeing how her shoulders relaxed and her nervous energy dissipated as she stared at the pulpit and the lilac-colored organ chamber — I realized that underneath all her anthropological accuracy lay genuine faith.
“You believe it all, right?” I asked. “Heaven. Hell. Souls.”
“Yeah, I do,” she answered softly, adding a moment later: “It makes things harder and easier.”

Life is easier with faith, she explained in a whisper, because if you truly believe in the gospel, then you understand that you’re already saved. “It’s like: ‘It’s done. So you’re good.’” But then, she added, if you sincerely believe that you’re saved, then why aren’t you doing all the good that you can as a saved person in this world?
“It means this responsibility. That’s why it’s so hard, but at the same time it’s so easy,” she said. “It’s actually walking as if you are fully loved.”
“By God?”
“Yeah, by God.” She glanced at my face, raised her eyebrows and smiled. “I know. I can see why people don’t believe it.”
I had known for a long time that Lee reads the Bible every morning before she writes — a habit inspired by Willa Cather — but in other interviews she’d explained it as an interest in biblical sentence structure and tone.
“That’s how it began,” Lee clarified now, suggesting that over time the purpose changed.
In America, there’s a tendency to see nonwhite novelists as ethnographers, and to overlook the more philosophical ambitions of their work. Yet Lee, like many of the 19th-century novelists, is also a moralist, and to think of her only as a Korean chronicler of the Korean diaspora is to misread her deeper project. “American Hagwon” contains clear indictments of education and materialism in America and Korea. Those bold plot lines, however, also lure readers into a more subtle consideration of the place that power, status, love, sacrifice, God and family hold in modern society. I had been puzzled at Lee’s home in Harlem when she told me that what she wanted to communicate to readers in her new novel was “the love that you need to feel a sense of sacrifice.”

“Smell that?” The novelist Min Jin Lee closed her eyes and drew in a breath. Garlic, ginger, turmeric, old floor polish, stale sweat, rat poison, glass cleaner, oregano. “It doesn’t smell like that on the Upper East Side,” she said with a laugh.
We were standing in the foyer of the apartment building on Van Kleeck Street, in Queens, where Lee lived with her parents and two sisters after they arrived from Korea in 1976. Everything looked the same: the dull metal mailboxes, the checkered linoleum in the hallway, the dusty glass wall facing the street. Only the names marking the buzzers had changed. In Lee’s childhood, they were mostly Irish, Greek and Eastern European. Now they were mostly Latino, Korean and Chinese.
The first thing that struck Lee about her new home was its ugliness. In Seoul, her mother kept their home impeccable. In Queens, their first rental was a one-bedroom furnished with grimy rugs, roaches and mice. Even at 7 years old, she understood that her family’s move to New York meant that they’d come down in the world.
In Seoul, they lived in a comfortable house in a middle-class neighborhood. Her father worked as a marketing executive. Her mother, who had studied music at Korea’s prestigious Yonsei University, taught children piano. But her father, who lost his home and most of his family as a teenager during the Korean War of the 1950s, feared that the violence of the Vietnam War might spread to South Korea and hurt his children. A relative in New York sponsored the family for visas, and they decamped for America, where her parents eventually found work in a wholesale jewelry shop in Midtown Manhattan. Every morning except Sunday they left the apartment at 6 to catch the subway, while the girls readied themselves for school alone.
For Lee, the move proved a social nightmare. In Korea, she’d been a peaceful introvert, the kind of child who often sat alone daydreaming. In America, she became a target. Tall, shy, not yet fluent in English, dressed in hand-me-downs, she was bullied ruthlessly for five years, starting in second grade.

“I was like a mark,” Lee recalled. “It was just like, You want to pick the big, goofy, quiet one.” Terrified, she turned nearly mute in public.
At home, though she was loved, she also felt there was something wrong with her. Her two sisters immediately tested into top academic classes, while she was tracked into the lowest classes for two years. Her father nicknamed her Turtle.
She had one superpower. At the age of 3, Lee taught herself to read. And in Queens, she discovered America’s great, humble treasure: the public library system. For an immigrant girl with no money, nowhere to go and no friends besides her sisters, the existence of a place that would lend her as many books as she wanted — for free! — was paradise. She read endlessly, rolling volumes home in a collapsible shopping cart. “A book only gives,” she explained to me. As a girl reading, she felt “infinite.” She became especially well versed in the classics of American and European literature, because those were the books the librarians recommended.
Now 57, Lee is considered one of the most important novelists of her generation — and a torch bearer for the great 19th-century tradition of social realism. Like George Eliot, she has a gift for combining intimate character portraits with sweeping macroeconomic narratives. Like Charles Dickens, she seems determined to expose the indignities of poverty and the resilience needed to survive them.

But even as she inherited her tools from these social realists, she uses them in modern ways to chronicle the lives of Koreans around the world. She set her first novel, “Free Food for Millionaires” (2007), among the Korean diaspora in New York City. The book’s central character, Casey Han, lives on Van Kleeck Street, until she escapes to Princeton and Manhattan. Lee’s second novel, “Pachinko” (2017), is a saga about four generations of Koreans. Set in colonial and post-colonial Japan, the novel is grounded in interviews that Lee conducted with elderly Koreans around Osaka and Tokyo. For her, “Pachinko” was a passion project; she never believed that it would find a big readership. After it was published, however, the novel became a global best seller and a critical sensation. In 2024, The New York Times Book Review ranked “Pachinko” No. 15 on its “100 Best Books of the 21st Century.”
“The fact that I can make that interesting to a general audience is really just a testament to what all those dead writers have taught me,” Lee told me. Her third novel, “American Hagwon,” debuted this month. Set in Korea, Australia and California during the years surrounding the Asian financial crisis of 1997, it contains more than a dozen characters from several interconnected families. The word “hagwon” means “private tutoring center” in Korean, and the novel examines how an unbridled obsession with gaining admission to name-brand universities may damage both parents and children. Among the book’s characters are parents who erase their savings paying for hagwons, teachers who coach SAT prep at hagwons and a young girl whose parents abandon her in California with the expectation that she will study hard, get accepted to U.C.L.A. and become a doctor — so that she can save her family in Korea from poverty.

For Lee, fiction has always been a way to wrestle with big social and historical dilemmas. Unlike many novelists, she begins her books with ideas and issues, not characters and scenes. Her chosen medium — the class-crossing realist narrative — has a long history as a weapon of social critique. Edith Wharton used it to savage the hypocrisies of old-money New York. Upton Sinclair used it to provoke reform in the slaughterhouses of Chicago. In “American Hagwon,” Lee herself is trying to shift the way we understand the purpose of higher education and to demonstrate how seemingly crazy behavior, like dropping off a 9-year-old in a foreign country, may be driven by a tremendous sense of fear and economic impotence.
When I asked Lee about the possibility of writing as a form of self-expression, she winced. “That’s not even interesting to me,” she said. “It sounds sort of corny, but if I didn’t think that these stories had value to my reader, I would never share it. Never.”
“History has failed us, but no matter.” The first line of “Pachinko” is a declaration of resilience and defiance, the pronouncement of someone who knows the score yet still forges ahead. The sentence is often interpreted as an indictment of the way historians tend to ignore the less-documented lives of the poor and the defeated. It may also be read as a wry summary of Lee’s own journey to “Pachinko.”

Inspired by classes that she took in African American studies and women’s studies, Lee spearheaded a campaign to persuade Yale to offer courses in Korean language and history. She had the ingenious idea of asking students to petition their parents for the changes rather than plead with the administration directly. One of these parents, she said, ultimately raised $100,000 for a pilot program. More than 20 years later, Yale still teaches Korean language as a result of these efforts.
Despite this triumph, Lee’s affair with history ended badly. During her junior year, the university finally offered the class on Korean history that she’d longed for. But when the professor returned her midterm exam, she felt socked. Lee’s blue book, she told me, contained no guiding corrections or annotations. On its last page, there was only one handwritten line — “Ah, me, what’s to say?” — next to the letter F.
Most of the students crying near her in class that day were Asian. So Lee asked the professor, a white man who specialized in Japanese history, for a demographic breakdown of the grades. When he presented it at the following class, it was clear that most of the students he’d failed were, in fact, Asian. The reason, he said, was that they were STEM majors. Outraged by his assumptions, Lee published an article in a campus newspaper detailing the incident. It raised a furor at Yale. A white student labeled her a politically correct “terrorist.” After that, she told me, students and professors in the history department regarded her as a troublemaker.
“I think my heartbreak was proportionate with how much I really wanted the class, which sounds so dorky,” Lee told me. She wasn’t worried about her grades. What she wanted was to be treated with respect. She passed the class, but after the scandal she couldn’t stomach approaching any professor in the department for a recommendation to a doctoral program.

At Yale, Lee had won two literary prizes: one for short fiction, the other for an essay. When she initially submitted the same essay to a history professor, he gave it a C and suggested that she needed remedial English tutoring. But the literary contests were hosted by the university’s English department, which scrubbed students’ names from their entries before judging. During that time, Lee’s writing earned her approximately nothing. She and Duffy, meanwhile, accumulated the joyous responsibility of caring for their first child and the unexpected necessity of supporting his parents through catastrophic debt. Her acute hepatitis recurred, making her wrists so weak that she had trouble lifting coffee cups. In a prologue to the 10th-anniversary edition of “Free Food for Millionaires,” she remembers her apprenticeship as an extended humiliation. “It is never a financially prudent idea to be a fiction writer,” she explains. “After six years, I had not yet written a published novel, and I was broke from the choices I had made.”
Because she was young and liver transplants were hard to obtain, a gastroenterologist suggested that she try an experimental drug: Interferon alfa. At the same time, she kept trying to compose the kind of juicy, realist book that enthralled her as a child. Lee often names “dead writers” as her teachers, including Leo Tolstoy, George Eliot, Edith Wharton, the Bröntes, Willa Cather, F. Scott Fitzgerald and James Baldwin. She read, reread and reverse-engineered their books. But in her prologue to “Free Food for Millionaires,” Lee recognizes that a host of contemporary authors taught her, as well. She took classes at the Asian American Writers’ Workshop and the 92nd Street Y in New York City, and participated in a private workshop with several aspiring writers, including the novelist Sharon Pomerantz, who remains a close friend. “You could look back on it with nostalgia,” Pomerantz said of this period in their lives, “but I think we were both filled with terror.”
From her legal experience, Lee carried over two unfashionable traits. The first was an attitude of advocacy. “This is the one part about being a lawyer I didn’t mind,” she told me. “I was arguing for somebody else.” All her novels are composed in defense of the overlooked, the tormented, the powerless. Though she published “Pachinko” a decade after “Free Food for Millionaires,” she worked on both books simultaneously. In one, Lee exposed the pressures and hypocrisies that Korean professionals faced in New York City. In the other, she laid bare an entire history of discrimination against Koreans in Japan. She felt as if she needed to write these stories for the sake of other Koreans, and this sense of responsibility kept her researching and revising even when the tasks she set for herself seemed absurdly hard.
“I would love to have that sort of freedom of saying, Oh, I don’t care what I stand for, but whether I like it or not, I do represent a group,” she said. “People still see you as the envelope that you’re in, whether you like it or not.”

The setting is an influential Presbyterian megachurch in Seoul’s fashionable Gangnam neighborhood. Its main pastor, an affable, 50-something man, is preaching on the sin of idolatry. His sermon opens with Leviticus: the Israelites who disobeyed God by sacrificing their children to a pagan deity. “What do you love more than your child?” the pastor asks his rich congregants. “What do you love more than God?”
His questions resonate throughout “American Hagwon,” but in this chapter, Lee treats them lightly, directing our attention mostly away from the pulpit and toward the pews.
A pair of sisters, Helen and Sonya, sit near each other with their two husbands, their five children and a father-in-law. Lee establishes their back story in two tight paragraphs. As girls, they “lived at subsistence level.” Their parents were gamblers, and they survived on charity from the Catholic Church. After they graduated from a prestigious women’s college, the gorgeous Sonya went to work for a real estate baron, who married her to his nephew. At the church, Sonya sports an elegant cashmere suit with “a thick rope of rare Tahitian pearls.” Helen wears a fancy wool suit that’s getting a little tight; Sonya bought it for her years earlier. Another woman, Nari, appears near the end of the chapter with her daughter. When Nari stands next to the sisters, she realizes that her expensive red dress with “dramatic black sequin flowers” looks tacky in church. She introduces Helen to the idea of sending her children to a budget-breaking hagwon.
These scenes don’t feel especially significant the first time you read them. But within a few hundred pages, two of these characters will be broke and working at a fried-fish joint in California. Another pair will be entangled in an eye-popping affair. Two acquaintances will have turned into best friends. And the six children will have attended five different universities on three different continents. One of them will drop out.

These are the techniques that Lee gleaned from the old social realists: intricately braided story lines, characters who cross social classes, an emphasis on plots that expose true morals. Many also deployed a nearly invisible third-person narrator. In “American Hagwon,” this device is so neutral as to be disconcerting. Flaubert eyed his characters — even those based on himself — with sly condescension. Dickens regarded his with sticky sentimentality. Lee’s vision is like bright, afternoon light; it casts no shadows. The rhythm of her sentences is conversational, and their diction is deliberately plain, barely adorned. It’s as if she wants to make reading her long, complicated novel as easy as possible, knowing that its most moving effects are felt not in the paragraphs but across the arc of chapters.
In college, Lee spent her most meaningful hours hanging out in the basement of Durfee Hall, where students of color held gatherings at the women’s center. The legacy of those sustaining female friendships appears in her work, where women are often rescued from hardship and despair by other women. In this sense, Lee’s books have more in common with Elena Ferrante’s Neapolitan novels than with anything by Eliot or Wharton.
“There’s a lot of different ways to circumvent patriarchy, because it’s such a heavy machinery,” Lee told me. “Whatever oppressive system you have, we get around it through other interpersonal relationships.”
Lee’s next novel is likely to push this theme even further. In our conversations, she referred to it as her “Marshall Plan book.” It would explore, she said, how the post-World War II rise of South Korea in the 1960s was underwritten by remittances sent home by Koreans living abroad, including culture-crossing wives. “When we think about all the glamour and beauty of South Korea today, we don’t think about all the bar girls who married G.I.s, who lived in Texas, and people called them hookers,” Lee said. “But if it weren’t for them, they wouldn’t have sponsored citizenship for their cousins and their brothers and sent money back for their education.”

It was hard for Lee to think about these women because it was so upsetting how they were mistreated. They sacrificed so much and, in return, they were slurred by other Koreans. It was too outrageous. She’d already begun filling a set of floor-to-ceiling shelves in her office with volumes of research.
One afternoon, Lee and I stood on Queens Boulevard staring at the Gothic face of the First Presbyterian Church of Newtown in Elmhurst. “This is the church I grew up in,” Lee said. “I remember thinking it was so much bigger.”
The bell tower seemed to waver in the July heat. In front, a wrought-iron gate was padlocked but a side door was cracked open. We slipped in.
“Nothing has changed,” Lee said, as she took a seat. Rib-like ceiling trusses graced a soaring ceiling; the stained-glass windows shimmered. The nave held no more than 20 pews. It smelled of wood polish and old velvet.
You could call this sanctuary Lee’s most important school. Together with her family, she attended services and youth groups, ate coffee cake and doughnut holes. Back then, the congregation was mostly Anglo American, but at Sunday school, unlike elementary school, people were nice to her.
Churches have always played a central function in Lee’s fiction. Her halls of worship allow characters to swap information, forge friendships, rustle up business, preserve their traditions and repair the damage done to their dignity by the turbulence of emigration. But sitting next her in the silence of First Presbyterian — seeing how her shoulders relaxed and her nervous energy dissipated as she stared at the pulpit and the lilac-colored organ chamber — I realized that underneath all her anthropological accuracy lay genuine faith.
“You believe it all, right?” I asked. “Heaven. Hell. Souls.”
“Yeah, I do,” she answered softly, adding a moment later: “It makes things harder and easier.”

_Calico Captive_, written by Elizabeth George Speare, is a 274-page historical novel set at the outbreak of the French and Indian War. In August 1754, Miriam Willard — a teenage girl living in Charlestown, New Hampshire — is taken captive along with her pregnant sister Susanna Johnson, Susanna’s husband James, and their three young children during an Abenaki raid. What follows is a harrowing march northward through the wilderness toward Canada, during which Susanna gives birth on the trail and names her newborn daughter Captive. After weeks of forced march, the prisoners arrive in Montreal, a city of French colonial intrigue and shifting wartime loyalties. There Miriam, by a sudden turn of fortune, is taken in by the prominent Du Quesne family, where she discovers a society utterly unlike anything in her New Hampshire experience. The novel is based directly on a true story: the captivity narrative of Susanna Johnson, whose account was published in 1807. Published in 1957 by Houghton Mifflin and Elizabeth George Speare’s first novel — she would go on to win two Newbery Medals, for _The Witch of Blackbird Pond_ (1959) and _The Bronze Bow_ (1962), and to receive the Laura Ingalls Wilder Award in 1989 — _Calico Captive_ remains in print and in classroom use nearly seventy years after its publication. Like the Speare novels that won greater recognition, it engages questions of cultural encounter, captivity, identity, and survival in colonial New England. Like the Speare novels, it also reflects the perspective of a white New England author of the mid-20th century, which teachers and parents should engage with rather than ignore. This complete guide covers _Calico Captive_‘s reading level, recommended age, content, key figures, themes, the representation question, and similar books — designed for parents, teachers, and students.

### For Parents
A gripping historical novel about a teenage girl’s captivity during the French and Indian War — well-paced, historically grounded, and the first novel by one of America’s most celebrated children’s historical fiction writers. Ages 10–14, grades 5–8. Content includes captivity, the hardships of forced wilderness march, and period-accurate depictions of colonial conflict. The book uses period-era terminology for Indigenous people that reflects its 1957 publication date.

### For Teachers
A grades 5–8 historical fiction text for French and Indian War units — one of the few children’s novels set in this period and directly based on a primary source. Speare’s prose is excellent and the historical research is solid. The depiction of the Abenaki people reflects 1957 assumptions and terminology; the guide to teaching the book well includes that conversation. Best paired with primary sources from the period and Indigenous perspectives on the conflict.

## What Reading Level Is Calico Captive?
_Calico Captive_ has a Lexile of 900L and an ATOS level of 6.0, with a Guided Reading Level of S. These scores place it at approximately a grades 5–7 independent reading level — consistent with the publisher’s interest level (grades 4–8) and with its widespread use across those grades. Speare’s prose is clear and assured — more direct than the high Lexile might suggest, with short declarative sentences in the action sequences and more complex construction in the Montreal scenes that reflect the social world Miriam is navigating. The 900L reflects the overall complexity of the vocabulary and sentence structure across the full novel.
Our editorial assessment places it at grades 5–8, ages 10–14. The wilderness march section reads quickly despite its difficulty; the Montreal section requires more patience as Miriam learns the social codes of French colonial society. Both sections reward the historical reader who brings some context to the French and Indian War period. For official Lexile and AR scores, visit Lexile.com or AR BookFinder. ReadingVine’s assessments are independent editorial judgments.

## What Age Is Calico Captive Appropriate For?
We recommend _Calico Captive_ for readers ages 10–14, grades 5–8. The primary content considerations are historical: the captivity narrative involves the realities of forced march through wilderness, captivity, the hardships of war, and the loss of autonomy. Susanna’s childbirth on the march is handled with restraint but present. The fate of some of the captives — separation, sale, and in some cases permanent loss of freedom — is depicted with historical directness. Nothing is gratuitous; the book is a 1957 children’s novel and reflects that era’s conventions about what to show young readers. The representation question regarding the Abenaki is addressed in its own section below.

## The True Story Behind Calico Captive
The novel is based directly on the historical record of the Johnson family captivity. In August 1754, a party of Abenaki warriors raided the settlement of Charlestown, New Hampshire — then known as Number Four — and took several colonists captive, including James Johnson, his pregnant wife Susanna, their three young children, and Susanna’s teenage sister Miriam Willard. The captives were marched northward to Canada, where they were sold to French colonists. Susanna Johnson gave birth during the march — the baby she named Captive survived. The family spent years in captivity in Montreal before eventually being ransomed and returned to New England.
Susanna Johnson herself wrote an account of the captivity, which was first published in 1807 as _A Narrative of the Captivity of Mrs. Johnson_. This document — a primary source in the captivity narrative tradition that was a significant genre of colonial American literature — is the direct basis for Speare’s novel. Speare followed the historical record faithfully for the major events and invented the texture of daily experience, the romantic subplot, and the interior life of Miriam Willard, whose perspective is central to the novel but who left no separate written account.
The captivity narrative as a genre — first-person accounts of colonial Americans captured by Indigenous people, published and widely read in the 17th and 18th centuries — was one of the most popular forms of literature in early America. Speare’s fictional retelling draws on this tradition while adding the novelist’s tools of character development and narrative pacing.

## What Is Calico Captive About?
It is August 1754 in Charlestown, New Hampshire. Miriam Willard, seventeen years old, is at her sister Susanna’s house — Susanna, very pregnant, and her husband James Johnson, and their three young children. The day holds the promise of Phineas Whitney, Miriam’s sweetheart, who is on his way to Harvard. Then comes the raid. The Abenaki warriors come swiftly; within hours the Johnsons, Miriam, and several other settlers are captives, marching northward through the forest toward Canada.
The march is brutal — icy streams, meager rations, the relentless pace, and the terror of what waits at the end. Susanna gives birth during the march. She names the baby Captive. The prisoners manage the wilderness with difficulty and courage; some do not survive the journey. When they arrive in Montreal, the French colonial capital, the family is separated and sold to different households. Miriam, through a stroke of fortune, ends up in the household of Madame Du Quesne, a wealthy and sophisticated French woman whose world is entirely foreign to Miriam’s Puritan New England upbringing.
Montreal is a revelation: French fashion, Catholic religion, formal social codes, music, dancing, the pleasures of a wealthy colonial city. Miriam adapts, learns, and finds herself drawn to Pierre Laroche, a young Frenchman — a complication for a girl whose heart and loyalties have always been with Phineas Whitney and New England. The novel follows Miriam’s years in Montreal as she works toward her family’s freedom, navigates competing loyalties and identities, and ultimately makes her choices about who she is and where she belongs.

## Elizabeth George Speare’s Legacy
_Calico Captive_ was Speare’s first novel, published when she was forty-nine years old — she had written magazine articles about family life before turning to historical fiction for children. The novel was recognized as an ALA Notable Book but did not win the Newbery; her next two novels would. _The Witch of Blackbird Pond_ (1959), also set in colonial New England and also about a girl navigating an unfamiliar culture, won the Newbery Medal in 1959. _The Bronze Bow_ (1962), set in first-century Judea, won the Newbery Medal in 1962 — making Speare one of only five authors in Newbery history to win the medal twice. _The Sign of the Beaver_ (1983) received a Newbery Honor and the Scott O’Dell Award for Historical Fiction. In 1989 she received the Laura Ingalls Wilder Award for her distinguished and enduring contribution to children’s literature. She died in 1994.
The themes and tensions of _Calico Captive_ — cultural encounter in colonial New England, a young woman navigating between worlds, the question of where she belongs — run through all of Speare’s major work. Kit Tyler in _The Witch of Blackbird Pond_ faces the same essential situation as Miriam Willard: brought from one culture into another, forced to navigate new codes and loyalties, uncertain which self is her true one. Reading the two books together is the most productive Speare author study available at this level.

## Books Similar to Calico Captive
**Island of the Blue Dolphins**
Scott O’Dell · Grade 5–7 · Ages 10–14
A girl alone in an extreme situation, surviving through courage and resourcefulness over years of isolation — the closest structural companion among books about female protagonists facing long-term captivity or isolation in the colonial period. Both novels are about the specific endurance required to survive in conditions you did not choose; both are based on real historical events; and both have been examined for their perspective on Indigenous people. Scott O’Dell and Elizabeth George Speare were the same generation of children’s historical fiction writers working in similar territory.
**Number the Stars**
Lois Lowry · Grade 4–7 · Ages 9–12
A girl navigating extreme historical circumstances in a city under occupation, hiding her true identity, making choices that require genuine courage — the same essential situation as Miriam in Montreal. Both novels are about female protagonists who find unexpected capacities in themselves under historical pressure, and both use a specific historical conflict (the French and Indian War; the German occupation of Denmark) as the context for a personal story about identity and survival.
**Hatchet**
Gary Paulsen · Grade 5–7 · Ages 10–14
A wilderness survival narrative — the march to Canada in Calico Captive and Brian’s survival in the Canadian wilderness share the same physical demands and the same requirement of moment-to-moment resourcefulness under extreme conditions. Hatchet is the contemporary version of what Miriam and the Johnson family experienced on the trail, written from a single protagonist’s internal perspective rather than a historical novelist’s reconstruction.
**Amos Fortune, Free Man**
Elizabeth Yates · Grade 5–8 · Ages 10–14
Another 1950s historical novel about captivity and the long work of reclaiming freedom — published just three years before _Calico Captive_ and sharing its New England setting, its period prose style, and the same critical questions about a mid-century white author’s perspective on historical experiences of captivity and constraint. Reading both together as companion texts for a unit on colonial New England history and historical fiction’s responsibilities is the most productive classroom use of either book.
**My Father’s Dragon**
Ruth Stiles Gannett · Grade 1–4 · Ages 5–9

## Books Similar to Calico Captive
For younger readers who are drawn to the Calico Captive premise — a child rescuing someone captive through resourcefulness and a specifically chosen set of tools — but who are not yet ready for Speare’s historical complexity. Elmer Elevator’s mission to free the dragon is the younger, gentler version of the same essential story: someone who deserves freedom is held captive; someone who cares about them sets out to help.

## About Elizabeth George Speare
Elizabeth George Speare was born on November 21, 1908, in Melrose, Massachusetts. She attended Smith College and Boston University, trained as a high school English teacher, and married Alden Speare in 1936. She spent her early adult years raising two children in Connecticut before turning to writing in earnest in her forties. She published magazine articles about family life before discovering, as she described it, “a true story from New England history with a character who seemed to me an ideal heroine” — the story of the Johnson family captivity — which became _Calico Captive_, her first novel, published in 1957 when she was forty-nine.
The novels that followed secured her place among the most important American children’s historical fiction writers of the 20th century. _The Witch of Blackbird Pond_ (1959) won the Newbery Medal; _The Bronze Bow_ (1962) won the Newbery Medal again — making her one of only five two-time Newbery winners in the award’s history. _The Sign of the Beaver_ (1983) received a Newbery Honor. In 1989 she received the Laura Ingalls Wilder Award for her distinguished and enduring contribution to children’s literature. She died on November 15, 1994, in Tucson, Arizona.
All of Speare’s major historical fiction shares a central preoccupation: a protagonist placed between two cultures, forced to navigate loyalty, identity, and belonging across that divide. Miriam Willard in _Calico Captive_, Kit Tyler in _The Witch of Blackbird Pond_, and Matt in _The Sign of the Beaver_ face versions of the same essential situation — the encounter with cultural difference under extreme pressure — that Speare returned to across her entire career.

## Calico Captive: Frequently Asked Questions
### What reading level is Calico Captive?
Lexile 900L, ATOS 6.0, Guided Reading Level S. Our assessment: grades 5–8, ages 10–14. The prose is clear and assured; the historical content benefits from contextual scaffolding about the French and Indian War period. For official Lexile and AR scores, visit Lexile.com or AR BookFinder.

## Calico Captive: Frequently Asked Questions
### What is Calico Captive about?
In August 1754, seventeen-year-old Miriam Willard is taken captive in an Abenaki raid on Charlestown, New Hampshire, along with her pregnant sister Susanna Johnson and Susanna’s family. After a harrowing wilderness march to Canada, during which Susanna gives birth and names her baby Captive, the prisoners arrive in Montreal. Miriam ends up in the household of the wealthy Du Quesne family, where she navigates French colonial society while working toward her family’s freedom — and questioning her own loyalties and identity.

## Calico Captive: Frequently Asked Questions
### Is Calico Captive based on a true story?
Yes — it is based directly on the historical captivity of the Johnson family in 1754, documented in Susanna Johnson’s own _Narrative of the Captivity of Mrs. Johnson_, first published in 1807. Speare followed the major historical events faithfully and invented the texture of daily experience, the interior life of Miriam Willard, and the romantic subplot. The Johnson family, the raid, the march, Montreal, and the eventual ransom are all historical.

## Calico Captive: Frequently Asked Questions
### What other books did Elizabeth George Speare write?
_The Witch of Blackbird Pond_ (1959, Newbery Medal), about a girl from Barbados navigating Puritan Connecticut; _The Bronze Bow_ (1962, Newbery Medal), set in first-century Judea; and _The Sign of the Beaver_ (1983, Newbery Honor and Scott O’Dell Award), about a boy left alone in colonial Maine who is befriended by an Abenaki boy. All four novels explore cultural encounter in historical settings; _The Witch of Blackbird Pond_ is the most direct companion to _Calico Captive_ in themes and approach.

## Calico Captive: Frequently Asked Questions
### How does Calico Captive depict the Abenaki?
The Abenaki are depicted as threatening figures whose motivations are not developed, using period-era terminology (“Indians,” “squaw”) throughout. The novel follows the perspective of the English colonial captives and Susanna Johnson’s 1807 captivity narrative; it does not present the Abenaki perspective or context for their actions. Teachers using the book should supplement it with Abenaki and Indigenous perspectives on the French and Indian War period. See the Representation section of this guide.

Followed by _Catriona (1893)_
_**Kidnapped**_ is a historical fictionadventure novel by Scottish author Robert Louis Stevenson, written as a boys' novel and first published in the magazine _Young Folks_ from May to July 1886. The novel has attracted the praise and admiration of writers as diverse as Henry James, Jorge Luis Borges, and Hilary Mantel.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kidnapped_(novel)#cite_note-Mantel-1) A sequel, _Catriona_, was published in 1893.
The narrative is written in English with some dialogue in the Lowland Scots language.
_Kidnapped_ is set around real 18th-century Scottish events, notably the "Appin Murder" and the Highland Clearances, which occurred in the aftermath of the Jacobite rising of 1745. Many of the characters are real people, including one of the principals, Alan Breck Stewart. The political situation of the time is portrayed from multiple viewpoints, and the Scottish Highlanders are treated sympathetically.
The full title of the book is _Kidnapped: Being Memoirs of the Adventures of David Balfour in the Year 1751: How he was Kidnapped and Cast away; his Sufferings in a Desert Isle; His Journey in the Wild Highlands; his acquaintance with Alan Breck Stewart and other notorious Highland Jacobites; with all that he suffered at the hands of his Uncle, Ebenezer Balfour of Shaws, falsely so-called: Written by Himself and now set forth by Robert Louis Stevenson._

The novel opens in the (fictional) village of Essendean in the Ettrick Forest area of the Scottish Lowlands in 1751. The main character and narrator is 17-year-old[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kidnapped_(novel)#cite_note-2) David Balfour whose sole remaining parent, his father, has recently died. The minister of Essendean, Mr. Campbell, hands David a sealed letter left by his father with instructions that it be delivered to his father’s brother, Ebenezer, at his family's ancestral estate, the House of Shaws in Cramond. Mr. Campbell tells David that he believes the letter may well prove to be advantageous to him.
After two days' walk cross country, David arrives at the ominous House of Shaws. There he is confronted by the paranoid Ebenezer with a loaded blunderbuss. His uncle is miserly, living on "parritch" and small ale, and the House of Shaws itself is partially unfinished and somewhat ruinous. David is allowed to stay and soon discovers evidence that his father may have been older than his uncle, thus making David the rightful heir to the estate. Ebenezer asks David to get a chest from the top of a tower in the house but refuses to provide a lamp or candle. David is forced to scale the stairs in the dark and by sudden luck of lightning illuminating the night scene discovers that not only is the tower unfinished in some places, but the steps simply end abruptly and fall into an abyss. David concludes that his uncle intended for him to have an "accident", perhaps so as not to have to give over his nephew's inheritance.
David confronts his uncle, who promises to address the matter the next morning. A ship's cabin boy, Ransome, arrives the next morning and tells Ebenezer that Captain Hoseason of the brig_Covenant_ needs to meet him to discuss business. Ebenezer takes David to a pier on the Firth of Forth, where Hoseason awaits, and David makes the mistake of leaving his uncle alone with the captain while he visits the shore with Ransome. Hoseason later offers to take them on board the brig for a drink and a brief tour, and David complies, only to see his uncle returning to shore alone in a skiff. David is then immediately struck senseless.

David awakens, bound hand and foot, in the hold of the ship, and learns that per arrangement with David's uncle, the captain plans to sell him into indentured servitude in the Carolinas. But the ship encounters contrary winds, which drive her back toward Scotland. Fog-bound near the Hebrides, they strike a small boat. All of the small boat's crew are killed except one man, Allan Breck Stewart, who is brought on board and offers Hoseason a large sum of money to drop him off on the mainland. David later overhears the crew plotting to kill Alan instead. David and Alan barricade themselves in the roundhouse, where Alan kills the murderous helmsman and David wounds Hoseason. Alan then demonstrates his superior fighting skills as he easily kills five more men and intimidates the remaining crew into backing down.
Hoseason has no choice but to give Alan and David passage back to the mainland. David tells his tale to Alan, who in turn states that his birthplace, Appin, is under the tyrannical administration of Colin Roy of Glenure, the King's factor and a Campbell. Alan, who is a Jacobite agent and wears a French uniform, vows that should he find the "Red Fox" he will kill him.
The _Covenant_ tries to negotiate a difficult channel without a proper chart or pilot and is soon driven aground on the notorious Torran Rocks. David and Alan are separated in the confusion, with David being washed ashore on the isle of Erraid, near Mull, while Alan and the surviving crew row to safety on that same island. David spends a few days alone in the wild before getting his bearings.
David learns that his new friend has survived, and David has two encounters with beggarly guides: one who attempts to stab him with a knife, and another who is blind but an excellent shot with a pistol. David soon reaches Torosay, where he is ferried across the river, receives further instructions from Alan's friend Neil Roy McRob, and later meets a catechist who takes the lad to the mainland.
_Kidnapped_ sketch of route of ship and David's walk across Scotland
As he continues his journey, David encounters none other than the Red Fox, Colin Roy Campbell himself, who is accompanied by a lawyer, a servant, and a sheriff's officer. When David stops the Campbell man to ask him for directions, a hidden sniper kills the King's hated agent.

David is denounced as a conspirator and flees for his life, but by chance reunites with Alan. The youth believes Alan is the assassin, but Alan denies responsibility. Alan and David then begin their flight through the heather, hiding from government soldiers by day. As the trek drains David's strength, his health rapidly deteriorates; by the time they are set upon by wild Highlanders who are sentries for Cluny Macpherson, an outlawed chief in hiding, the lad is barely conscious. Alan convinces Cluny to give them shelter, and David is tended by a Highland doctor. He soon recovers, though in the meantime Alan loses all of their money at cards with Cluny, only for Cluny to give it back when David practically begs for it.
When David and Alan resume their flight in cold and rainy weather, David becomes ill again, and Alan carries him on his back down the burn to reach the nearest house, fortuitously that of a Maclaren, Duncan Dhu, who is both an ally of the Stewarts and a skilled piper. David is bedridden and given a doctor's care, while Alan hides nearby, visiting after dark.
In one of the most humorous passages in the book, Alan convinces an innkeeper's daughter from Limekilns (unnamed in _Kidnapped_ but called "Alison Hastie" in its sequel) that David is a dying young Jacobite nobleman, despite David's objections, and she ferries them across the Firth of Forth. There, they meet a lawyer of David's uncle's, Mr. Rankeillor, who agrees to help David properly claim his inheritance. Rankeillor explains that David's father and uncle had once quarrelled over a woman, David's mother, and the older Balfour had married her, informally giving the estate to his brother to settle their dispute while living as an impoverished schoolteacher with his wife. This agreement had lapsed with his death.

There, they meet a lawyer of David's uncle's, Mr. Rankeillor, who agrees to help David properly claim his inheritance. Rankeillor explains that David's father and uncle had once quarrelled over a woman, David's mother, and the older Balfour had married her, informally giving the estate to his brother to settle their dispute while living as an impoverished schoolteacher with his wife. This agreement had lapsed with his death.

texts.0: _Calico Captive_, written by Elizabeth George Speare, is a 274-page historical novel set at the outbreak of the French and Indian War. In August 1754, Miriam Willard — a teenage girl living in Charlestown, New Hampshire — is taken captive along with her pregnant sister Susanna Johnson, Susanna’s husband James, and their three young children during an Abenaki raid. What follows is a harrowing march northward through the wilderness toward Canada, during which Susanna gives birth on the trail and names her newborn daughter Captive. After weeks of forced march, the prisoners arrive in Montreal, a city of French colonial intrigue and shifting wartime loyalties. There Miriam, by a sudden turn of fortune, is taken in by the prominent Du Quesne family, where she discovers a society utterly unlike anything in her New Hampshire experience. The novel is based directly on a true story: the captivity narrative of Susanna Johnson, whose account was published in 1807. Published in 1957 by Houghton Mifflin and Elizabeth George Speare’s first novel — she would go on to win two Newbery Medals, for _The Witch of Blackbird Pond_ (1959) and _The Bronze Bow_ (1962), and to receive the Laura Ingalls Wilder Award in 1989 — _Calico Captive_ remains in print and in classroom use nearly seventy years after its publication. Like the Speare novels that won greater recognition, it engages questions of cultural encounter, captivity, identity, and survival in colonial New England. Like the Speare novels, it also reflects the perspective of a white New England author of the mid-20th century, which teachers and parents should engage with rather than ignore. This complete guide covers _Calico Captive_‘s reading level, recommended age, content, key figures, themes, the representation question, and similar books — designed for parents, teachers, and students.

### For Parents
A gripping historical novel about a teenage girl’s captivity during the French and Indian War — well-paced, historically grounded, and the first novel by one of America’s most celebrated children’s historical fiction writers. Ages 10–14, grades 5–8. Content includes captivity, the hardships of forced wilderness march, and period-accurate depictions of colonial conflict. The book uses period-era terminology for Indigenous people that reflects its 1957 publication date.

### For Teachers
A grades 5–8 historical fiction text for French and Indian War units — one of the few children’s novels set in this period and directly based on a primary source. Speare’s prose is excellent and the historical research is solid. The depiction of the Abenaki people reflects 1957 assumptions and terminology; the guide to teaching the book well includes that conversation. Best paired with primary sources from the period and Indigenous perspectives on the conflict.

## What Reading Level Is Calico Captive?
_Calico Captive_ has a Lexile of 900L and an ATOS level of 6.0, with a Guided Reading Level of S. These scores place it at approximately a grades 5–7 independent reading level — consistent with the publisher’s interest level (grades 4–8) and with its widespread use across those grades. Speare’s prose is clear and assured — more direct than the high Lexile might suggest, with short declarative sentences in the action sequences and more complex construction in the Montreal scenes that reflect the social world Miriam is navigating. The 900L reflects the overall complexity of the vocabulary and sentence structure across the full novel.
Our editorial assessment places it at grades 5–8, ages 10–14. The wilderness march section reads quickly despite its difficulty; the Montreal section requires more patience as Miriam learns the social codes of French colonial society. Both sections reward the historical reader who brings some context to the French and Indian War period. For official Lexile and AR scores, visit Lexile.com or AR BookFinder. ReadingVine’s assessments are independent editorial judgments.
texts.4:
## What Age Is Calico Captive Appropriate For?
We recommend _Calico Captive_ for readers ages 10–14, grades 5–8. The primary content considerations are historical: the captivity narrative involves the realities of forced march through wilderness, captivity, the hardships of war, and the loss of autonomy. Susanna’s childbirth on the march is handled with restraint but present. The fate of some of the captives — separation, sale, and in some cases permanent loss of freedom — is depicted with historical directness. Nothing is gratuitous; the book is a 1957 children’s novel and reflects that era’s conventions about what to show young readers. The representation question regarding the Abenaki is addressed in its own section below.
texts.5:
## The True Story Behind Calico Captive
The novel is based directly on the historical record of the Johnson family captivity. In August 1754, a party of Abenaki warriors raided the settlement of Charlestown, New Hampshire — then known as Number Four — and took several colonists captive, including James Johnson, his pregnant wife Susanna, their three young children, and Susanna’s teenage sister Miriam Willard. The captives were marched northward to Canada, where they were sold to French colonists. Susanna Johnson gave birth during the march — the baby she named Captive survived. The family spent years in captivity in Montreal before eventually being ransomed and returned to New England.
Susanna Johnson herself wrote an account of the captivity, which was first published in 1807 as _A Narrative of the Captivity of Mrs. Johnson_. This document — a primary source in the captivity narrative tradition that was a significant genre of colonial American literature — is the direct basis for Speare’s novel. Speare followed the historical record faithfully for the major events and invented the texture of daily experience, the romantic subplot, and the interior life of Miriam Willard, whose perspective is central to the novel but who left no separate written account.
The captivity narrative as a genre — first-person accounts of colonial Americans captured by Indigenous people, published and widely read in the 17th and 18th centuries — was one of the most popular forms of literature in early America. Speare’s fictional retelling draws on this tradition while adding the novelist’s tools of character development and narrative pacing.
texts.6:
## What Is Calico Captive About?
It is August 1754 in Charlestown, New Hampshire. Miriam Willard, seventeen years old, is at her sister Susanna’s house — Susanna, very pregnant, and her husband James Johnson, and their three young children. The day holds the promise of Phineas Whitney, Miriam’s sweetheart, who is on his way to Harvard. Then comes the raid. The Abenaki warriors come swiftly; within hours the Johnsons, Miriam, and several other settlers are captives, marching northward through the forest toward Canada.
The march is brutal — icy streams, meager rations, the relentless pace, and the terror of what waits at the end. Susanna gives birth during the march. She names the baby Captive. The prisoners manage the wilderness with difficulty and courage; some do not survive the journey. When they arrive in Montreal, the French colonial capital, the family is separated and sold to different households. Miriam, through a stroke of fortune, ends up in the household of Madame Du Quesne, a wealthy and sophisticated French woman whose world is entirely foreign to Miriam’s Puritan New England upbringing.
Montreal is a revelation: French fashion, Catholic religion, formal social codes, music, dancing, the pleasures of a wealthy colonial city. Miriam adapts, learns, and finds herself drawn to Pierre Laroche, a young Frenchman — a complication for a girl whose heart and loyalties have always been with Phineas Whitney and New England. The novel follows Miriam’s years in Montreal as she works toward her family’s freedom, navigates competing loyalties and identities, and ultimately makes her choices about who she is and where she belongs.
texts.10:
## Elizabeth George Speare’s Legacy
_Calico Captive_ was Speare’s first novel, published when she was forty-nine years old — she had written magazine articles about family life before turning to historical fiction for children. The novel was recognized as an ALA Notable Book but did not win the Newbery; her next two novels would. _The Witch of Blackbird Pond_ (1959), also set in colonial New England and also about a girl navigating an unfamiliar culture, won the Newbery Medal in 1959. _The Bronze Bow_ (1962), set in first-century Judea, won the Newbery Medal in 1962 — making Speare one of only five authors in Newbery history to win the medal twice. _The Sign of the Beaver_ (1983) received a Newbery Honor and the Scott O’Dell Award for Historical Fiction. In 1989 she received the Laura Ingalls Wilder Award for her distinguished and enduring contribution to children’s literature. She died in 1994.
The themes and tensions of _Calico Captive_ — cultural encounter in colonial New England, a young woman navigating between worlds, the question of where she belongs — run through all of Speare’s major work. Kit Tyler in _The Witch of Blackbird Pond_ faces the same essential situation as Miriam Willard: brought from one culture into another, forced to navigate new codes and loyalties, uncertain which self is her true one. Reading the two books together is the most productive Speare author study available at this level.
texts.11:
## Books Similar to Calico Captive
**Island of the Blue Dolphins**
Scott O’Dell · Grade 5–7 · Ages 10–14
A girl alone in an extreme situation, surviving through courage and resourcefulness over years of isolation — the closest structural companion among books about female protagonists facing long-term captivity or isolation in the colonial period. Both novels are about the specific endurance required to survive in conditions you did not choose; both are based on real historical events; and both have been examined for their perspective on Indigenous people. Scott O’Dell and Elizabeth George Speare were the same generation of children’s historical fiction writers working in similar territory.
**Number the Stars**
Lois Lowry · Grade 4–7 · Ages 9–12
A girl navigating extreme historical circumstances in a city under occupation, hiding her true identity, making choices that require genuine courage — the same essential situation as Miriam in Montreal. Both novels are about female protagonists who find unexpected capacities in themselves under historical pressure, and both use a specific historical conflict (the French and Indian War; the German occupation of Denmark) as the context for a personal story about identity and survival.
**Hatchet**
Gary Paulsen · Grade 5–7 · Ages 10–14
A wilderness survival narrative — the march to Canada in Calico Captive and Brian’s survival in the Canadian wilderness share the same physical demands and the same requirement of moment-to-moment resourcefulness under extreme conditions. Hatchet is the contemporary version of what Miriam and the Johnson family experienced on the trail, written from a single protagonist’s internal perspective rather than a historical novelist’s reconstruction.
**Amos Fortune, Free Man**
Elizabeth Yates · Grade 5–8 · Ages 10–14
Another 1950s historical novel about captivity and the long work of reclaiming freedom — published just three years before _Calico Captive_ and sharing its New England setting, its period prose style, and the same critical questions about a mid-century white author’s perspective on historical experiences of captivity and constraint. Reading both together as companion texts for a unit on colonial New England history and historical fiction’s responsibilities is the most productive classroom use of either book.
**My Father’s Dragon**
Ruth Stiles Gannett · Grade 1–4 · Ages 5–9
texts.12:
## Books Similar to Calico Captive
For younger readers who are drawn to the Calico Captive premise — a child rescuing someone captive through resourcefulness and a specifically chosen set of tools — but who are not yet ready for Speare’s historical complexity. Elmer Elevator’s mission to free the dragon is the younger, gentler version of the same essential story: someone who deserves freedom is held captive; someone who cares about them sets out to help.
texts.13:
## About Elizabeth George Speare
Elizabeth George Speare was born on November 21, 1908, in Melrose, Massachusetts. She attended Smith College and Boston University, trained as a high school English teacher, and married Alden Speare in 1936. She spent her early adult years raising two children in Connecticut before turning to writing in earnest in her forties. She published magazine articles about family life before discovering, as she described it, “a true story from New England history with a character who seemed to me an ideal heroine” — the story of the Johnson family captivity — which became _Calico Captive_, her first novel, published in 1957 when she was forty-nine.
The novels that followed secured her place among the most important American children’s historical fiction writers of the 20th century. _The Witch of Blackbird Pond_ (1959) won the Newbery Medal; _The Bronze Bow_ (1962) won the Newbery Medal again — making her one of only five two-time Newbery winners in the award’s history. _The Sign of the Beaver_ (1983) received a Newbery Honor. In 1989 she received the Laura Ingalls Wilder Award for her distinguished and enduring contribution to children’s literature. She died on November 15, 1994, in Tucson, Arizona.
All of Speare’s major historical fiction shares a central preoccupation: a protagonist placed between two cultures, forced to navigate loyalty, identity, and belonging across that divide. Miriam Willard in _Calico Captive_, Kit Tyler in _The Witch of Blackbird Pond_, and Matt in _The Sign of the Beaver_ face versions of the same essential situation — the encounter with cultural difference under extreme pressure — that Speare returned to across her entire career.
